The air inside the Palladium was electric, thick with the nervous energy of a thousand waiting audience members and the suffocating heat of a hundred stage lights. 

Standing in the center of the famous red stage was twelve-year-old Leo Vance. Clad in a slightly oversized denim jacket, holding a microphone in a hand that wouldn't stop trembling, he looked impossibly small. Behind the scenes, his mother stood with Ant and Dec, clutching her hands so tightly her knuckles were white.

"Hello," Simon Cowell said, his voice echoing through the auditorium. He leaned forward, resting his chin in his hand, looking at the boy over the rim of his glasses. "What’s your name?"

"L-Leo," the boy squeaked into the mic. He cleared his throat, trying again. "Leo Vance, sir."

"And how old are you, Leo?"

"I'm twelve."

"And why are you here today?"

Leo took a shaky breath. "My granddad always told me I had a voice, but I was too scared to sing in front of people. He passed away last year... so I'm here to prove to him, and to myself, that I can do it."

A collective "Aww" rippled through the audience. Amanda Holden smiled warmly, while Alesha Dixon offered an encouraging nod. 

"Well, good luck, Leo. What are you going to sing for us?" Simon asked.

"I'm singing an uptempo dance-pop song," Leo replied, naming a current radio hit known for its heavy electronic beat and fast lyrics.

Simon raised an eyebrow, a flicker of doubt crossing his face, but he gestured toward the wings. "Whenever you're ready."

The backing track exploded through the venue’s speakers—a barrage of loud, synthesised bass and driving drums. Leo raised the microphone to his lips and began to sing. But almost instantly, it was clear something was wrong. 

The music was too fast. Leo was rushing to keep up with the rhythm, his voice sounding thin, swallowed whole by the overwhelming backing track. He was pitchy, visibly panicked, his eyes darting wildly around the room as he struggled to find his footing. Amanda looked pained; Bruno Tonioli winced slightly.

In the wings, Leo’s mum covered her mouth, tears welling in her eyes. It was turning into a disaster.

Suddenly, thirty seconds into the performance, Simon raised a single, flat palm into the air. 

He didn't hit his red buzzer, but he didn't need to. The floor manager instantly cut the audio. The backing track died mid-beat. 

A heavy, awkward silence fell over the Palladium. Leo froze, his eyes widening. A quiet murmur of disappointment ran through the crowd. The poor boy stood alone in the center of the quiet stage, looking utterly defeated, biting his lip to keep from crying.

Simon pulled the microphone closer. 

"Leo," Simon began, his tone sharp but calm. 

The audience braced themselves, expecting the trademark brutal critique.

"Leo... that was terrible," Simon said bluntly. The crowd gasped, a few scattered boos echoing from the upper balcony. Simon held up a hand to quiet them. "No, hear me out. Leo, that track was obnoxious. It was loud, it was frantic, and it was entirely wrong for you. You were fighting against a computer screen, and it was hiding who you actually are."

Simon leaned over his desk, locking eyes with the terrified twelve-year-old. "I can hear something in your voice, Leo, beneath all that noise. But that song was a mistake. Tell me you brought something else."

Leo swallowed hard, his voice barely a whisper. "I... I have a second song prepared, sir."

"What is it?"

"It's 'A Change Is Gonna Come' by Sam Cooke."

Simon’s eyebrows shot up. "A twelve-year-old singing Sam Cooke?" He paused, contemplating. "Okay. Here’s what we’re going to do. No heavy backing track. No dance beats. Just a piano. Can we get just a piano track, please?"

The sound booth confirmed with a thumbs-up. 

"Take a breath, Leo," Simon said, his tone softening significantly. "Forget about the judges. Forget about the audience. Forget about the cameras. Just sing it for your granddad. Whenever you're ready."

Leo closed his eyes. He took a long, slow breath, letting his shoulders drop. 

A single, melancholy piano chord chimed through the quiet auditorium. The room held its breath.

Leo opened his eyes, looked up toward the ceiling lights, and sang the opening line.

*"I was born by the river... in a little tent..."*

The transformation was instantaneous, and it was breathtaking. 

Without the loud synth track, Leo’s real voice soared through the theater. It was rich, soulful, and carried a raspy, emotional depth that belonged to a blues singer three times his age. Every note was infused with pure, unadulterated feeling.

Amanda’s jaw dropped. Alesha brought her hands to her mouth, goosebumps visibly rising on her arms. 

In the wings, Ant stared at the stage in disbelief. "Bloody hell," he whispered.

Leo built up to the chorus, his voice swelling with power he hadn't shown moments earlier:

*"It's been a long... a long time coming, but I know... a change gonna come..."*
